issues: The final sentence ('By the end of this teardown, you will know how to spot whether your own homepage is making the same trade') is a generic promise-of-value closer that could appear in almost any teardown intro — it does not anchor to Expensya's specific trade-off.
The word count is approximately 89 words — at the very top of the 55–90 word limit. One more clause would breach the cap.

The phrase 'That is not a translation. It is a different company talking to a different buyer.' makes a mild causal/interpretive leap presented as fact rather than as an observed signal — the evidence supports 'may suggest' language, not a declarative assertion.
No period label ('Oct 2020 to Jun 2026') appears in the intro. The section goal requires the period to be named.
requiredFixes: Add the period covered — 'Oct 2020 to Jun 2026' — somewhere in the paragraph. The section goal explicitly requires it, and it is currently absent.

Replace the generic closing sentence ('By the end of this teardown, you will know how to spot whether your own homepage is making the same trade') with a concrete, Expensya-specific closer — e.g. name the single biggest trade Expensya made (dropping 'Free trial' and English-first reach to own the French finance buyer) so the reader knows exactly what the teardown will examine.

Soften the declarative 'That is not a translation. It is a different company talking to a different buyer.' to signal it is an interpretation grounded in the evidence, not a confirmed strategic fact — e.g. 'That reads less like a translation and more like a different company addressing a different buyer entirely.'
riskFlags: 'That is not a translation. It is a different company talking to a different buyer.' — stated as fact; the evidence supports this as a reasonable inference but no confirmed strategy is documented. Needs hedging per the evidence notes.

'Expensya's English homepage is gone' — stated as absolute fact; the evidence shows French is now primary but an 'Anglais' language toggle exists in the new nav, suggesting English access persists. This claim may be technically inaccurate.

The H1 in the evidence ('How Expensya rewrote its homepage over 6 years') is weaker than the article heading used in the draft. The draft heading is the better SEO choice and should be preserved.

The intro does not surface any secondary keyword naturally (e.g. 'repositioning', 'localization', 'spend management software') — one organic secondary keyword mention would improve search snippet relevance without bloating word count.
rewriteInstruction: Keep the strong opening observation and the headline contrast — those are the best parts.
